text: There are n cars heading to mile target, each with a start position and a speed. A car can't pass another — it catches up and then travels at the slower car's speed, forming a fleet. Return how many fleets reach the target.

Thanks. Before I dive in, I'd like to clarify a few things. Just to make sure I'm understanding this correctly — whether two cars end up together depends on their arrival times, not raw speed, since they start at different places. And if they arrive at the target at the same instant, they count as one fleet. Right?

Key fact: a rear car A merges into a front car B exactly when A's time is less than or equal to B's time. A starts behind, so arriving no later means it must have caught up, and it can't pass. Time here is target minus position, divided by speed.

Hmm, let me think about this for a second. A naive approach would be to simulate positions over time and watch cars merge — messy and slow. This problem reminds me of a monotonic stack over sorted data, and it fits because each car only cares about which rear fleets it absorbs. So, sort by position and compare arrival times. I process cars from the back and keep a stack of fleet arrival times; a new front car absorbs any rear fleet whose time is less than or equal to its own.

Here's the plan. One: sort the car indices by position, and compute each arrival time as a double. Two: for each car, from back to front, pop every stacked time that is less than or equal to its time — those rear cars catch up and merge. Three: push its time, and return the stack size. One thing worth flagging — two correctness details. The time must be a double; integer division would collapse distinct arrival times and overcount merges. And I compare with less-than-or-equal, so cars that meet exactly at the target count as one fleet. Does this approach sound good, or would you rather I think of another way?

Alright, let me code this up. I'll think out loud as I go. I sort an index array by position, ascending. Then for each car I compute its time as a double, pop every stacked fleet whose time is less than or equal to it, and push the car's index with its time. The stack size is the answer. That matches the plan. One thing worth flagging — I sort indices, not the arrays, so position and speed stay aligned. The cast to double happens before the division; casting after would already be too late. The survivors on the stack are exactly the independent fleets.

Let's dry-run target twelve, positions ten, eight, zero, five, three, speeds two, four, one, one, three. Expected three fleets. Sorted by position, the times are twelve, three, seven, one, one. The row that matters is the car at five, with time seven: the car at three, with time three, is behind it, so it catches up and they arrive together at seven. The cars at eight and ten both arrive at one, and less-than-or-equal merges them. Three arrival times survive — three fleets. That matches. Corner cases: a single car is one fleet. If every car arrives strictly later than the car ahead, nobody catches up — n fleets.

The time complexity is n log n, dominated by the sort; the stack pass is linear. The space complexity is linear, for the index array and the stack. Oh, one more thing — I could drop the stack: sweep from the front to the back and keep one running current fleet time, counting each car whose time exceeds it. That's the same logic in constant extra space beyond the sort. And to avoid floating point entirely, I'd cross-multiply the time comparison.

Nicely done. Three things stood out. You judged merging by arrival time, not speed. You flagged the double and the less-than-or-equal as correctness requirements, not style. And you offered both the constant-space sweep and the cross-multiplication to avoid floats. Good work.
